words_with_history.title: Orð með sögu
text: Ásta heyrði nafnið Hrafnkell Freysgoði. Hún spurði: „Er hann goð?“ En afi sagði: „Nei, goðinn er maður.“
Goð er ekki maður. Freyr var goð, en Hrafnkell var goði. Hann var bóndi og prestur, og hann réð miklu. Hann gaf Frey gjafir.
Siggi vildi sögu um menn, ekki um goð. Afi sagði honum sögu um goða. Í sögunni voru menn og goð. Hrafnkell átti Freyfaxa með Frey.
words_with_history.note_en: Goði is derived from goð, “god”. In the Icelandic Commonwealth, a goði was a chieftain with religious associations. The conventional count of 39 goðorð refers to an early arrangement; their number and character changed over time. A goðorð was not simply a territorial parish.

grammar.note_en:
A reflexive pronoun points back to the subject of its own clause. A clause is a unit built around a verb; the subject is the person or thing doing or undergoing what that verb describes. In Hann meiddi sig á fæti (s052), “he hurt his leg”, both hann and sig refer to the horse. In Siggi … klæddi sig (s057), “Siggi got dressed”, sig refers to Siggi. The verb determines the object’s case: meiða sig and klæða sig use accusative sig; þvo sér, “wash oneself”, and flýta sér, “hurry”, use dative sér here. Einar hugsaði með sér (s078), “Einar thought to himself”, has dative after með. In Hrafnkell kallaði Einar til sín (s024), “Hrafnkell called Einar to him”, genitive sín follows til and refers to Hrafnkell, the subject, not Einar. There is no nominative reflexive: sig/sér/sín does not serve as the subject. These forms are the same for masculine, feminine and neuter, singular and plural. In the first and second persons, the ordinary personal pronoun serves reflexively: Þú þvoðir þér (s059), “you washed yourself”. Do not substitute third-person sér for second-person þér.

The possessive sinn means “his/her/its/their own”, referring back to the subject within the clause. It agrees in gender, number and case with the thing possessed, not with its owner. Siggi borðaði grautinn sinn (s060), “Siggi ate his own porridge”: masculine accusative sinn agrees with grautinn. Hann leit ekki á móður sína (s060), “he did not look at his mother”: feminine accusative sína agrees with móður. Bjarni fór … að hestinum sínum (s061), “Bjarni went out to his own horse”: masculine dative sínum agrees with hestinum. In hest föður síns (s032), “his father’s horse”, genitive síns agrees with genitive föður; the owner referred back to is Siggi. The outer noun hest is accusative but does not determine síns. Do not confuse genitive reflexive sín with a feminine or plural possessive form spelled sín; they belong to different pronouns.

Contrast Einar reið hesti hans, ekki sínum (s079), “Einar rode his [Hrafnkell’s] horse, not his own”. Hans names another male owner, Hrafnkell; sínum would make Einar the owner. Hans and hennar are invariant possessive genitives: they do not change to agree with the possessed noun. Ásta horfði á blautu skóna hans (s070), “Ásta looked at his [Siggi’s] wet shoes”, uses hans because Ásta is the subject and Siggi owns the shoes. Freyr var goðið hans (s016), “Freyr was his [Hrafnkell’s] god”, likewise refers to an owner outside the subject phrase. A possessive within the subject itself uses hans/hennar, not sinn in these ordinary clauses: hesturinn hans, “his horse”, is possible; hesturinn sinn cannot be used as an independent subject to mean “his own horse”. This is the requested hesturinn hans ↔ hesturinn sinn contrast: the second phrase is not a valid subject replacement. The story’s subject Hesturinn minn (s063), “my horse”, illustrates that possessive position without an unattested nominative sinn example. Sá hestinn sinn (s084) is instead an object, “saw his own horse”. The thought in s078 sets up the ownership contrast made explicit in s079. More complex reflexive reference in reported clauses comes later; this chapter practises the local pattern.

Complete personal-pronoun reference, for lookup only (not a claim that every cell occurs in this story). In each line the order is nominative / accusative / dative / genitive:
1st singular: ég / mig / mér / mín.
2nd singular: þú / þig / þér / þín.
3rd singular masculine: hann / hann / honum / hans; feminine: hún / hana / henni / hennar; neuter: það / það / því / þess.
1st plural: við / okkur / okkur / okkar.
2nd plural: þið / ykkur / ykkur / ykkar.
3rd plural masculine: þeir / þá / þeim / þeirra; feminine: þær / þær / þeim / þeirra; neuter: þau / þau / þeim / þeirra.
3rd-person reflexive, either number and any gender: — / sig / sér / sín.
The first-person and second-person genitives in this list are personal-pronoun forms; ordinary possession in the singular uses declining minn and þinn, not free mín/þín in every frame. The tables above contain only this chapter’s attested examples.

Formal address (þérun), recalled from Kafli 8, is a secondary reference here: þér / yður / yður / yðar, with second-person plural verb agreement. No priest appears and no formal address is demonstrated or drilled in this chapter. Ordinary dative singular þér in Þú þvoðir þér is a different use of the same spelling. All four pronoun cases are a reference, not a new paradigm-recitation task.
